The Story of Vrushabsen and the Wicked Minister

I bow to Lord Jinendra, the word of Jina, and the ocean of knowledge, the monks, and I write the excellent story of Vrushabsen.

In the south, in the city of Kundal, King Vaishravan was very righteous and possessed right faith. But his minister, Rishthamatra, was the complete opposite — a man of false faith who deeply hated Jain dharma. Truly, snakes always live around sandalwood trees.

One day, Shri Vrushabsen Muni came to Kundal Nagar with his monastic group. Hearing of his arrival, Vaishravan went forth with great splendour, accompanied by worthy souls, to pay his respects. With devotion, he circumambulated the monk, praised him, worshipped him with pure substances, and heard the Jain discourse on dharma. Hearing the discourse, he was greatly pleased. Truly, who among those worthy of a good destiny would not be happy upon hearing the discourse of this supreme dharma that bestows all happiness?

The royal minister too came to the monastic group — not to worship or praise them, but to engage in scriptural debate, to humiliate them, and to shake people's faith in them. But this was his mistake, for those who dig a pit for others fall into it themselves. And so it happened. The minister debated with the monks out of the desire to humiliate them, but he was the one who was humiliated. He lost the debate. The wound of this defeat struck deep in his heart. Resolved to take revenge, he came secretly to the monks' resting place that evening and set fire to the place where they were staying. It is deeply sad, but the nature of the wicked is peculiar — they first provoke others, and when they receive the fruit of their own actions, they think, "This one has wronged me," and become angry at innocent, good people, tormenting them in various ways to take revenge.

Whatever the case, the minister left no stone unturned in his wickedness. He created a terrible disturbance for the monastic group. But those monks — knowers of truth, understanders of the real nature of things — paid no heed to this suffering. They endured everything with great forbearance. In the end, according to the purity of their mental states, some attained liberation and some went to heaven.

The wicked man, however, could harm the saints no more than a serpent can harm a mountain. His evil deeds rebounded upon himself. After death, he fell into a terrible hell, where he suffered for countless ages. Eventually, through the ripening of residual merit, he regained human form and, through the grace of Jain dharma, found the path to liberation.

This story teaches that the wicked can never truly harm the saints. The monks' forbearance in the face of the minister's fire was their greatest victory. The minister's evil deeds only brought suffering upon himself. The wise should cultivate forbearance and never resort to violence, even when provoked. For in the end, the wicked destroy only themselves, while the saints rise ever higher on the path to liberation.
